sections.h2: What is a quick way to sell in Royal Palm Beach, FL?
sections.html:
Royal Palm Beach owners usually pick between two quick paths: an investor who accepts present condition, or a competitively priced listing with paperwork ready at the first showing. The listing reaches more people; the investor gives a firmer date.

The village is a municipality, but the property appraiser and the clerk who records your deed belong to Palm Beach County. Sellers lose time on small items such as an expired permit or an unfiled homestead change, so the sections below list checks worth doing first.

  • Gather the deed, any survey, and recent permit and inspection records.
  • Request a payoff letter from the mortgage holder.
  • Decide whether the house sells occupied or empty.

Royal Palm Beach serves about 40,000 residents in the central part of Palm Beach County, roughly 10 miles west of the Atlantic Ocean. The village designates its entire area a bird sanctuary and has been a Tree City USA since 1990.

For a seller, the trees and parks matter in practical ways: the village has a vegetation removal permit, and a house with mature landscaping or a lake easement may come with its own rules. Because the village sits inland, buyers touring a house here are weighing canals, lake easements and drainage rather than beach access. The village's forms include easement, lake easement maintenance and canal alert items for that reason.

sections.h2: Village forms and permits that come up before a sale
sections.html:
The village's Forms, Permits and Applications page is the best checklist for work on a house you are about to sell. It lists the documents the building and planning staff use, and several of them show up in buyer inspections.

sections.h2: What if the house has an open permit or a code complaint?
sections.html:
Ask the village building division to look up the address. The village has a request to administratively close a permit, a permit extension application and a code enforcement fine mitigation request form, so each situation has a set procedure.

A permit that was never finaled can surface when a buyer's inspector or lender pulls records. Closing it before listing is usually faster than negotiating it after you have an offer. A cash buyer will often take the house with whatever permit history exists and adjust the price, which can be the simplest path when the work is large.

  • Open permit: ask about closing, extending or finaling it.
  • Code fine: the village offers a fine mitigation request form and an agent authorization form.
  • Palm Beach County impact fees: the village links a county impact fee form for new construction questions.

Palm Beach County has no special deed rate, so the standard 70 cents per hundred dollars applies. Any loan staying on the property is counted in the price used (s. 201.02).

The clerk's per-page recording charge sits under s. 28.24, and your title agent will list both amounts at closing. The contract says who pays, though anyone on the deed remains answerable to the state.

Values lock in on January 1. The county tax collector mails bills in November, and paying that month earns 4 percent off, with the discount dropping a point each month until February. Unpaid bills turn delinquent on April 1.

Selling counts as a change of ownership, so the property returns to just value the next January 1. If you will buy again in Florida, portability can carry part of a Save Our Homes benefit to the new homestead. Ask the appraiser about the three-year window and Form DR-501T.

Renting out the house ends homestead for that period. Confirm which exemption sits on your parcel with the Palm Beach County Property Appraiser before signing.

• Missed payments: a court-ordered foreclosure sale lands 20 to 35 days after judgment (s. 45.031). A sale before that keeps equity with you.
  • Tenant in place: nonpayment draws a three-day notice that skips weekends and legal holidays (s. 83.56).
  • Inherited: a deed from a personal representative under a probated will is listed by the state as untaxed.

On closing day you sign the deed with two witnesses, review the settlement statement and hand over keys. The Palm Beach County clerk then records the deed, and your proceeds are released. A cash sale skips the buyer's appraisal and loan approval, so title and payoffs set the timeline.

Ask the title agent for a dated list of deadlines so you know which one controls.

sections.h2: What to gather before talking to buyers
sections.html:
Start with the paperwork that answers a buyer's first questions: the recorded deed, a survey if you have one, the last tax bill, and any permit finals for roof, windows, pool or shutters. The village's checklists for those items show what staff expect, so you can tell quickly whether your records are complete.

Next, find out whether a homeowners association or lake or canal easement applies to the lot. An association can add its own approval and fee steps that lengthen a closing. Finally, request a payoff letter from your lender. With those four pieces in hand, a cash buyer can price the house in a day or two, and a listing agent can write accurate disclosures.

  • Recorded deed and survey
  • Latest tax bill and homestead status
  • Permit finals and warranties
  • Payoff letter and association contact

sections.h2: Proving the work was done right
sections.html:
The village publishes a Single Family Home Checklist, a Planning and Zoning Pre Review Checklist and a Home Improvement Guidelines sheet on working with contractors. Reading them shows what staff look for on a finished house.

It also has forms for a Private Provider request and results guideline, which some owners use when a private firm does the inspections. If your records mention a private provider, keep the results with the sale papers.

  • Waiver and Release of Lien forms, partial and final, prove a contractor was paid.
  • The Final Acknowledgement form closes out a job.
  • An Elevation and Drainage Certification Compliance form applies where grading matters.

Buyers rarely read these forms themselves, but their inspectors and title agents often ask whether lien releases exist for recent work.

faqs.q: Which office records my Royal Palm Beach deed?
faqs.a: The Palm Beach County clerk records it. The village does not record deeds, though its building division holds permit records that buyers ask about.

faqs.q: Is the stamp tax different in Palm Beach County?
faqs.a: No. Only Miami-Dade has a different rate, so the 70 cents per $100 deed rate applies in Palm Beach County.

faqs.q: Can I sell if the village has a code fine on the house?
faqs.a: Yes. The village offers a fine mitigation request form, and a payoff or lien search at closing will show any balance. Ask the village code enforcement office for the current status.

faqs.q: Does a tree come down without village approval?
faqs.a: Often not. The village has a Vegetation Removal Permit, so ask the village before cutting anything on the lot.

faqs.q: How long does a homestead exemption last after I sell?
faqs.a: It ends with the sale. The new owner has to file their own application by March 1, and the property goes to just value the next January 1.
